questions.stem: The operations `push(4)`, `push(9)`, `push(2)`, `pop()`, `push(7)`, `pop()` are applied to an initially empty stack. What does the **second** `pop()` return?
questions.explanation: A stack is last-in-first-out, so `pop` always removes the most recent surviving push. After pushing 4, 9, 2 the top is 2, which the first `pop` removes. Pushing 7 then makes 7 the top, so the second `pop` returns 7. The stack afterwards holds 4 and 9 with 9 on top.

distractorRationale.a: 2 was returned by the *first* pop, not the second
distractorRationale.b: 4 is at the bottom and would be returned last under LIFO discipline
distractorRationale.d: 9 becomes the top only *after* the second pop removes 7

questions.stem: A queue is initially empty. After `enqueue(A)`, `enqueue(B)`, `enqueue(C)`, `dequeue()`, `enqueue(D)`, `dequeue()`, which element is at the front?
questions.explanation: A queue is first-in-first-out, so `dequeue` removes the oldest element. The contents evolve as [A, B, C] → [B, C] after the first dequeue → [B, C, D] after enqueuing D → [C, D] after the second dequeue. C is therefore at the front and D at the rear.

distractorRationale.a: A was removed by the first dequeue
distractorRationale.b: B was removed by the second dequeue
distractorRationale.d: D is the newest element, so under FIFO it is at the rear; it would be at the front only under LIFO discipline

questions.stem: Evaluate the postfix (reverse Polish) expression `5 3 2 * + 4 -` using a stack. Give the result as a number only.
questions.explanation: Push operands and, on each operator, pop two operands and push the result — taking care that the *first* value popped is the right-hand operand. Trace: push 5, 3, 2; `*` pops 2 then 3 and pushes $3 \times 2 = 6$; `+` pops 6 then 5 and pushes $5 + 6 = 11$; push 4; `-` pops 4 then 11 and pushes $11 - 4 = 7$. The stack holds exactly one value, 7, which is the result. Postfix needs no parentheses because the operator order fixes the grouping.

questions.stem: A parser checks that brackets are correctly nested using a stack: push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket pop and compare. Which additional condition must be checked for the input to be accepted?

options.text: Nothing further — matching every closing bracket is sufficient
The stack must be empty when the input is exhausted
The stack must contain exactly one item when the input is exhausted
The total number of brackets must be even

questions.explanation: Two failure modes exist and the loop detects only one of them. A closing bracket with an empty stack or a mismatched top is caught inside the loop. But unclosed openings such as `([]` leave residue on the stack and never trigger a comparison, so acceptance requires the additional postcondition that the stack is empty at end of input.

distractorRationale.a: Accepts `([]`, which has every closing bracket matched but one opening bracket unclosed
distractorRationale.c: Would reject the correctly balanced `()`, whose stack is empty at the end
distractorRationale.d: An even count is necessary but not sufficient: `)(` has two brackets and is not balanced

questions.stem: A queue is implemented as a circular buffer over an array of capacity 8. The rear index is currently 7 and a slot is free. What is the rear index after the next `enqueue`?

options.text: 7 — the buffer must be reallocated instead

questions.explanation: Indices advance modulo the capacity: $\text{rear} = (\text{rear} + 1) \bmod 8 = (7 + 1) \bmod 8 = 0$. Wrapping is what makes the circular buffer work — without it the queue would drift towards the end of the array and report itself full while low-numbered slots stood empty, which is the defect of the naive two-index implementation.

distractorRationale.b: Index 8 is out of bounds for a capacity-8 array; the modulo is exactly what prevents this
distractorRationale.c: Applies the modulo to the wrong quantity, as if the increment were 2
distractorRationale.d: Reallocation is needed only when the buffer is genuinely full, and the question states a slot is free

questions.stem: In a circular buffer that tracks only a front and a rear index, the completely full and completely empty states are indistinguishable, so an explicit count or one sacrificed slot is required.
questions.explanation: True. With $c$ slots there are $c + 1$ possible occupancies (0 to $c$) but only $c$ distinct values of the difference $(\text{rear} - \text{front}) \bmod c$, so by counting alone two states must collide — and the colliding pair is full and empty, both giving $\text{front} = \text{rear}$. The two standard remedies are to store the element count explicitly, or to declare the buffer full at $c - 1$ elements so that $\text{front} = \text{rear}$ unambiguously means empty.

questions.stem: A graph traversal keeps a frontier of discovered-but-unexplored vertices. Which choice of container yields which traversal?

options.text: A stack gives breadth-first search; a queue gives depth-first search
A queue gives breadth-first search; a stack gives depth-first search
Both containers give breadth-first search; the difference is only in memory use
Neither: the traversal order depends solely on the adjacency list ordering

questions.explanation: The frontier's removal discipline is the traversal. A queue removes the oldest discovered vertex, so the search finishes all vertices at distance $d$ before any at distance $d+1$ — that is breadth-first, and it is why BFS finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph. A stack removes the newest, so the search plunges along one branch until it dead-ends — that is depth-first. The two algorithms are otherwise identical code.

distractorRationale.a: Inverts the correspondence: LIFO deepens the search, FIFO widens it
distractorRationale.c: The orders differ fundamentally; only BFS visits vertices in non-decreasing distance from the source
distractorRationale.d: Adjacency ordering decides which sibling is visited first, but not whether the search proceeds by level or by branch

questions.stem: The values 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed onto a stack in that order, with `pop` operations interleaved freely. Which output sequence is **impossible**?
questions.explanation: For 4 to be output first, 1, 2 and 3 must all be on the stack with 3 on top, so the remaining outputs are forced to be 3, 2, 1. The sequence 4, 1, 2, 3 would require reaching 1 from the bottom of the stack while 2 and 3 sit above it, which LIFO forbids. The general rule is that a sequence is achievable exactly when no output value is followed later by two values in increasing order that were both pushed before it.

distractorRationale.b: Push 1, 2, 3; pop three times; push 4; pop
distractorRationale.c: Push 1, 2; pop (2); push 3, 4; pop (4); pop (3); pop (1)
